sentences.text: The only known species of this dinosaur is H. australis, a name combining the Mapudungun word for duck with the Greek word for lizard to honor its southern origin.
This herbivore is estimated to have reached a length of around 8 meters.

Originally named in 1984 from Late Campanian to Early Maastrichtian fossils found in the Los Alamitos Formation of Río Negro Province, Patagonia, Argentina, the species was initially called "Kritosaurus" australis.
A 2022 study recognized it as a distinct genus separate from Secernosaurus and other Kritosaurini members, proposing the new name Huallasaurus to distinguish it from North American Kritosaurus.
CT scans revealed that Huallasaurus vertebrae had a relatively dense trabecular architecture and lacked invasive pneumaticity in the centra, neural arches, and neural spines.
The lack of invasive air sacs in Huallasaurus vertebrae supports the hypothesis that air sac diverticula did not evolve in Ornithischia and suggests a "pelvic bellows" ventilation mechanism.
Huallasaurus may have supported its large body size and fat reserves through a combination of dense trabecular bone, thin cortical walls, and the absence of invasive air sacs.

The internal vertebral structure of Huallasaurus is more similar to silesaurs like Silesaurus than to other archosauriforms, though it is debated whether this indicates a deep phylogenetic relationship or convergent evolution.
While Huallasaurus vertebrae superficially resemble those of large mammals with expanded trabecular matrices and thin walls, the functional equivalence of these structures is speculative.
Huallasaurus is classified in the family Hadrosauridae and belongs to the parent group Kritosaurini.

Rozadilla et al. (2022) recovered Huallasaurus within a clade consisting entirely of South American saurolophines, which was named Austrokritosauria and is recovered as the sister taxon to Kritosaurini.

Phylogenetic analysis recovers a new clade of South American hadrosaurs composed of Kelumapusaura machi, Huallasaurus australis, Bonapartesaurus rionegrensis, and Secernosaurus koerneri, supported by traits including a subhorizontal crest on the ilium, a longitudinal crest on the dorsal surface of the postacetabular process, and a twisted distal end of the postacetabular process.

Huallasaurus lived during the Late Cretaceous, approximately between 73 and 69 million years ago, specifically during the Maastrichtian stage from 72.2 to 66 million years ago, in what is now South America.
Huallasaurus fossils are known from the Late Cretaceous Los Alamitos Formation of Río Negro Province, Argentina, where the sauropod Aeolosaurus rionegrinus has also been found.
